1:
A song breaks into the judgments, and they explain the interruption differently. Calvin makes it relief: the prophet had these calamities almost before his eyes, and since a man who fears God trembles at any token of anger, the confused emotions would have overwhelmed him had he not taken refuge in praise. Delitzsch calls it an echo, the prophet transported to the end of the days as choral leader of the church to come, whose psalms do not merely repeat the prophecy but sink into it and draw more out. Clarke doubts any close connection with the chapter before, whose subject was desolation, but finds one across the run from the thirteenth onward. Wesley says the prophet, reflecting on what he had delivered, broke off. Ellicott hears the burst as Paul's, praise following a sight of the heavenly city.

The counsels are old, the works new. Henry keeps both halves: the wonders surprise us and were unthought of, yet were devised long since, every operation of providence running by eternal counsels which are faithfulness and truth themselves. Wesley has them conceived from eternity and revealed from time to time. Ellicott would drop the supplied verb and read the counsels of old in apposition with the wonders, the missing conjunction sharpening the list. Gill fastens on the opening claim, that God is his by covenant and not only creation, and reports the Jewish commentators disputing whether the speaker is the prophet or the church's elders.

Which city is the heap nobody settles. Clarke offers Nineveh, Babylon, Ar of Moab or any fortress of the enemies, and adds that the versions cannot agree on number, some reading the city and others cities. Calvin thinks the singular stands for many, a change customary with the prophets, and dismisses the reading that made Jerusalem the palace. Wesley agrees one is put for many, the cities carrying their countries and kingdoms with them. Gill rejects Samaria and Jerusalem, prefers Babylon, then prefers Rome, citing Jerome for the Jewish reading and the Targum for the plural. Ellicott alone holds the historical and typical together: Nineveh or Babylon in the prophet's thought, but that city standing for the world-power of every age, so his Babylon becomes the type of the later.

The palace of strangers divides them again. Clarke reads the proud for the strangers, one letter apart and easily confused, the Greek behind him. Wesley keeps the strangers, Gentiles whose palaces stood in royal cities. Calvin refuses foreigners moving into captured towns, since the next clause says it shall be no city; he hears irony, and puts highwaymen in the palaces because the emptied place has room for anyone. Then the strong people glorify. Henry allows two readings, enemies converted or at least made to own themselves beaten, or a weak people made strong and terrible for God. Calvin makes the conversion the point: destruction alone would produce only horror, and praise flows from a sense of goodness.

The last figures are weather. Gill makes the strength given the poor inward: love shed abroad, grace upheld. Calvin turns poverty into a condition: only there does God find means of kindness, so he trains us by the cross until we can receive it. Ellicott renders the strength a fortress, the oppressor's fierceness heat and an eastern tornado dashing at a wall. Clarke would read a winter storm, and rebuilds the comparison as a thick cloud tempering the sun over burnt ground. Calvin canvasses three ways of taking the heat and chooses a fourth, a shower quenching what would consume us. Ellicott notes the Greek reading Zion where the Hebrew has a parched place, and closes on the last word: not the branch of the terrible ones but their song, a rare noun found so in the Song, blighting the world till it too is hushed. Wesley keeps the branch, an arm.
6:
Calvin clears two readings away before anyone eats. Some make it a threat, the Gentiles invited to prey on the Jews as beasts are fattened for slaughter. Others make the drink the cup of wrath and the guests drunk on it. He refuses both without long refutation, holding the prophet to be going on with the grace revealed at Christ's coming, borrowing the psalm where poor and rich sit down together and are satisfied. Clarke reads the same, a feast being the usual expression of joy after victory, and finds confirmation in what follows, the unveiling being the preaching of the gospel and the abolished death immortality procured. Ellicott makes his point about the prophet: it is characteristic of him to see the outlying nations admitted rather than shut out.

The provisions are read as closely as the guest list. Clarke renders the wines on the lees old wines, kept long on their sediment, the word for lees meaning the preservers, because they keep the strength and flavour in. Calvin says the same, calls the common rendering inaccurate, and compares what the French call long-kept wines, better than ordinary in the east where they carry their age; yet the liquid holds no dregs. Wesley splits the difference: left on the lees a competent time, then drawn off and refined. Henry attends to the host: God prepares as becomes him to give, not as becomes us to receive, and where the feast of Ahasuerus was for show, all here is substance.

Then the covering, and here they part. Delitzsch denies it means mourning and makes it spiritual blindness, the veil that lay on Israel's heart. Calvin agrees, noting that others take it for the disgrace under which believers live unrecognised; the veil is ignorance, and the gospel is commended for dispelling the dark. Wesley localises the same blindness, on the Gentiles then and the Jews now. Gill fills it in: the darkness spread by Mahomet and by Rome, and above all human doctrines and traditions. Ellicott keeps the mourning: in the East a covered face meant grief for the dead, so destroying it defeats death, though he lets the other sense mingle. Clarke instead unveils the Mosaic ritual, shown by the apostles to have pointed at one sacrifice.

Which death is swallowed, and when. Gill works by elimination, ruling out spiritual death, the conversion of the Jews and the civil death of the witnesses, settling on the bodily, abolished at the cross and finished at the resurrection. Henry will not let it be the Assyrian rout or the return from Babylon alone, since by Paul's word the saying is brought to pass at our rising, which he calls the key to the promises here. Wesley distinguishes two deaths, the sting of the first taken, the second prevented. Delitzsch says the feast is on earth, but an earth made heaven, the wall between God and the world fallen. Calvin asks outright where this is fulfilled, when we die daily and the chief pillars of the church were treated as sweepings; his answer is the whole reign of Christ, stretched to the second coming.

The tears and the reproach go last. Ellicott traces the words back to an earlier prophet and forward to Paul's anthem and the Apocalypse, and makes the reproach the taunt of the day of affliction, where is now their God. Calvin makes the removal structural: happiness needs perpetuity and joy alike, a life that ends being wretched at its height and one without gladness making death preferable; glory is added because a people held in contempt would trust the promise less. Clarke turns the passage into three headings, plenty, light and comfort, then supplies the image he thinks underlies it: in Arabia the condemned man's face was covered, and the world was being led to execution when a sacrifice procured a general pardon.
9:
The verb has no subject, so they supply one. Clarke reports the Greek and Latin reading a plural, they shall say, the Syriac a second person, and takes the speakers for Jews and Gentiles together. Calvin notes the form is indefinite and renders it passively, the saying belonging to nobody and to everyone. Ellicott finds the speakers obvious, the redeemed citizens of the new city, their supplications turned to anthems. Henry hears four things at once: that God must have the glory, since triumph may not stop at the gift but pass to the giver; that long waiting makes the arrival more welcome; that the joy is unspeakable; that having saved he will go on saving. Wesley reads recognition, the long-promised one come with salvation in his hand.

Calvin turns the shout into an argument about certainty. That the cry is public is proof the grace was received, the banquet not prepared in vain if men are heard feasting. He presses it: the revelation will be clear enough to fix the mind on God's word without hesitation, so Christians may say with the woman at the well that they worship what they know. He sets the fathers' dim knowledge under the law against the fullness shining in the gospel, and allows himself a flourish, away with all the inventions of men. Gill dates the scene, putting the saying at the glorious appearing, when the feast is spread and the veil gone.

Then the hand rests, and an unexpected name arrives. Calvin insists the hand means assistance not chastisement, and rest the unbroken continuance of protection, rejecting those who read judgment on the Jews; God scatters blessings over the world, but his hand rests only where he is worshipped. Wesley says the presence has its settled abode. Clarke would repoint the verb to read that the hand shall give rest, on the Greek and the Coptic. Ellicott admits Moab looks like a descent from an apocalypse over death to a local quarrel; his answer is the Moabite stone, where Chemosh is set against Israel's God, making the name representative, so there was a mystical Moab as later a mystical Babylon. Calvin gets there by synecdoche, adding that enemies somewhat related to us do the most damage.

The treading is agricultural, and Clarke stops to explain the machine. Meadow and hay being scarce, they chop straw for cattle with heavy iron-toothed wheels drawn over open threshing floors till the stalks are cut to chaff; so Moab is crushed until nothing whole is left in him. Delitzsch keeps the wetter image the text gives, straw trodden into the water of a dung pit, and sets two pictures across the Jordan, which he calls the great gulf of the parable, mercy one side and wrath the other. Ellicott hears a pun, finding in the word for dunghill the name of a Moabite town, so the place becomes an unconscious prophecy of its own fate.

The swimmer is the last dispute. Ellicott lays out three readings, God spreading his hands with a swimmer's strength to hold Moab down, the hands stretched on the cross, and Moab thrashing in deep water; each has supporters, and he judges the last the most fitting. Clarke agrees and goes further, repointing the participle to one who is sinking, since he cannot see how a swimming stroke illustrates God reaching out to destroy, and reads the struggle as public, watched by the neighbouring nations. Gill and Wesley keep it God's hand, Wesley adding that Moab can no more resist it than water resists a swimmer. Calvin keeps it God's too, for an unexpected reason: swimmers do not lunge, they spread and draw back gently and still cut the water, and so God destroys the well-armed without armies or noise. On the walls all agree, and Calvin ends counselling patience till the appointed time.
